director.chapterArc: A survivalist transition from passive waiting to active labor, anchored by a flashback that recontextualizes Jab's magical ability (the Kindling) not as heroic power but as functional utility. The emotional core shifts from the physical exhaustion of rain and fever to the quiet devastation of parental loss.
director.restraintNote: Maintain clinical precision during the technical descriptions of shelter repair and blade formation; do not romanticize the magic or the ceremony. When Jab delivers the news of his parents' death, strip all dramatic inflection—read it as a logistical update rather than an emotional outburst to preserve the character's survivalist logic.

cues.delivery: Narrative voice shifts to a warm, observational tone during the flashback. The rhythm should be steady and rhythmic, mimicking the flow of water and memory. Avoid melodrama in the dialogue; let the characters' competence speak for itself.
cues.from: They did it at the low water, after the racks were full.
cues.through: It went on. Eleven people, in the end. He had not expected eleven. He had expected his parents and his aunt and perhaps the old man, and instead they kept starting up out of the crowd, and one of them was a woman he had only ever spoken to about her dog, and she said, mine, I taught him to swim, and he was a coward about it for one whole summer and then he was not, and Jab stood in the water with his face burning in the cold and understood, in a way that he had not understood at any point in thirteen years of living among them, how much of him had been put there on purpose by other people's hands.
cues.reason: Flashback sequence requires distinct tonal separation from present-day survival.

cues.delivery: Dry, understated delivery for the child's reaction. The humor lies in the contrast between the solemn ceremony and a baby laughing at an ugly blade.
cues.from: Tonk was ten months old. He had two teeth and no opinions about anything except being put down. He came awake at the light and stared at it over their mother's shoulder with his mouth open, and then he reached for it — one fat hand out into the air, grabbing, the way he grabbed at the fire and the smoke and the rain and everything else that had ever been beautiful and bad for him — and he laughed.
cues.reason: Brief moment of levity that highlights tragedy.

cues.delivery: Flat, factual delivery. Jab speaks to Tonk as a partner in survival; no condescension or dramatic pause for grief.
cues.from: "She died when the bridge went," Jab said. "In the water. Dad too. They're not coming, and I'm not going to tell you they are."
cues.through: Tonk's face did nothing at all. That was what it did. He was four and the fever was on him and the information went in and found nothing to attach to, and he looked past Jab's shoulder at the fir branches for a while.
cues.reason: Critical pivot point where emotional restraint defines the character.

Emphasis on the pragmatic rule of the ceremony.

pauses.after: It went. He did not see it go. There was no moment where it was visible and then was not; there was only a hook in his fingers and then cold water running through empty fingers, and a small unreasonable lurch under his ribs that he had not been prepared for at all.
pauses.reason: Emotional landing on the physical sensation of loss during the offering ritual.
Isolating the physical sensation of loss during the ritual.

pauses.after: It was not large. That was the part he had never once been told and later told everyone — a warmth the size of a coin, low, under the breastbone and a finger's width behind it, in a place he had gone thirteen years without having any reason to notice. Then a second warmth started up in his hand, the right one, down in the meat of the palm. And then, with no gap between the two things at all, came the knowing: those were not two warmths. They had never been two. They were one warmth that had been in him the whole time, and the only new thing in the world was that they were now in the same room and could see each other.
pauses.reason: Major revelation regarding the nature of Jab's power; allow processing time.
Critical realization about Jab's power; isolates the concept for clarity.

pauses.before: What Jab had was a fish knife.
pauses.reason: Emphasis on the disappointing reality of his magical form.

pauses.after: He did not call it. Nothing about it was his idea. A line woke up along the working edge and ran outward from his hand, thin as a hair and the low amber color of a coal with ash on it — and two-thirds of the way along, at the fat part of the belly, it stuck. It guttered there. It went out and came back and went out, three times, at that one curve, while sixty people watched, and Jab's whole face went hot and he thought, with total clarity, it can't even do it properly.
pauses.reason: Dramatic landing on the blade's failure to ignite perfectly; emphasizes realism over heroism.
Father's validation focuses on utility over aesthetics; isolates the key phrase.

pauses.after: "Well, it looks like you," she said. "That's the whole of it. You'll spend a while wishing it looked like somebody else. Don't spend too long."
pauses.reason: Return from flashback to present day; reset narrator stance and emotional distance.
Emphasis on the precariousness of his temporary repair.

pauses.after: He put it in the ledger with the salve and the fish and the nineteen — seventeen — twists of bark, and went to check his brother.
pauses.reason: Completed thought on the inventory of supplies before shifting focus back to Tonk.

pauses.after: Tonk's face did nothing at all. That was what it did. He was four and the fever was on him and the information went in and found nothing to attach to, and he looked past Jab's shoulder at the fir branches for a while.
pauses.reason: Pause after Jab's statement about his parents' death; allows the weight of the fact to land without melodrama.
